docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Sources: hooks, plugin components, dependencies, plugin CLI.

  • Rules: a plugin SessionStart hook's stdout, or hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, is added to context. Matchers startup|resume|clear|compact re-inject after /clear and compaction. Over 10,000 characters, Claude sees a 2,000-character preview only. A plugin-root CLAUDE.md, rules, and most settings are not loaded. claude plugin validate accepts the hook (checked here); that the text reaches the model is unconfirmed (needs a live session).
  • Packs: "dependencies": [{"name": "brainrc", "version": "^0.3"}] installs core with a pack; versions resolve to git tags <plugin>--v<version>. claude plugin list --json lists installed plugins with their paths. A pack skill dispatching a core agent across plugins is unconfirmed.
  • Hooks from several plugins all run; deny > ask > allow.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
Source: openai/codex at 529cd6b (the docs site was blocked here): codex-rs/core-plugins/, codex-rs/hooks/, codex-rs/agent-roles/.

  • Reads .claude-plugin/marketplace.json and .claude-plugin/plugin.json as well as its own .codex-plugin/. Verified with Codex 0.161.0: codex plugin marketplace add <repo> and codex plugin add brainrc@brainrc install our plugin unchanged. Gatework's plugin (brainrc/gatework) works the same way. The install copy drops symlinks (skills/brainrc-gatework/roles), so spec-agent falls back to ../../agents/.
  • Skills come from the manifest's skills field when it has one, and only from there, so Gatework's names ./skills/ as one string, the form Codex's docs give. Core's own plugin has no skills.
  • Skills: native, ~/.agents/skills (~/.codex/skills deprecated). Custom prompts are deprecated for skills; a plugin's commands/ become skills, except any that use $ARGUMENTS (verified: all five of ours were skipped). Core now ships them as user-invoked skills, which Codex installs.
  • Hooks: PreToolUse, SessionStart, and more, from a plugin's hooks/hooks.json. Whether a SessionStart hook can inject rules is unconfirmed.
  • Agents: [agents.<role>] TOML; a plugin can't ship them.

docs.title: Antigravity CLI
docs.text:
Google's docs site was blocked here and agy (closed source) couldn't be installed, so this comes from public sources: the antigravity-cli CHANGELOG and issues (#403, #1053, #1059), and plugins that record tested behavior (MemPalace, CoalHearth v2.8.0 on agy 1.3.1). Nothing here was run against a real agy.

  • A plugin is a folder with plugin.json (its schema requires name and rejects unknown keys; a skills path or list adds skill folders to skills/, and nothing names other folders), plus optional skills/, agents/, rules/, hooks.json, and mcp_config.json. agy plugin install <git url> needs plugin.json at the repo root. No commands/: skills are the slash commands. Install may copy only the folders it recognises (#403).
  • Rules: rules/*.md load only with frontmatter naming a trigger (always_on, model_decision, glob, manual); files without one are dropped silently.
  • Hooks: hooks.json at the plugin root, {"<name>": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher", "hooks"}]}}; commands run from the plugin folder. PreToolUse gets toolCall: {name, args} (run_command → args.CommandLine; view_file, write_to_file, replace_file_content) and prints {"decision": "ask" | "deny", "reason"}. An empty {} is reported to deny every call and allow is documented as auto-approve, so a guard has no safe reply for "no objection". Not shipped until a live test settles it.
  • Skills: disable-slash-command hides a skill from /; disable-model-invocation is likely ignored.

docs.title: OpenCode
docs.text:
Source: sst/opencode docs source at a697115 (the docs site was blocked here): packages/web/src/content/docs/.

  • A plugin is a JS module: hooks (tool.execute.before), tools, and system-prompt transforms. It can't ship agent, skill, or command files, so the package is a config dir plus a small plugin.
  • Agents need a transform (#19, shipped in 0.3.19): Claude's tools: Read, Grep makes OpenCode's whole config invalid (verified, 1.18.35); it wants permission, model as provider/model-id, and mode: subagent.
  • Guard plugin: tool.execute.before can block by throwing and permission.ask can answer a prompt OpenCode already shows, but a plugin can't force a prompt, so "ask" becomes "deny".
  • Skills: native, ~/.config/opencode/skills/ (also reads ~/.claude/skills/).

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
cursor.com is blocked from where this was built, so the format comes from Cursor's official plugin repo, cursor/plugins (checked 2026-10-09 at ccb5507: schemas/, its plugins, and its create-plugin scaffold skill), plus hook payload types from the community cursor-hooks package.

  • Manifest: .cursor-plugin/plugin.json, only name required, unknown keys rejected. skills, agents, rules, commands take relative paths; hooks a path or an inline object. Our generated manifest validates against schemas/plugin.schema.json.
  • Local install: a plugin directory, or a symlink to one, at ~/.cursor/plugins/local/<name>/. A search result says Cursor falls back to .claude-plugin/ when .cursor-plugin/ is missing, so we ship our own: Cursor rejects Claude's hook format.
  • Rules: description, alwaysApply, optional globs frontmatter; Cursor's examples use .mdc. Whether a plugin loads .md rules is unconfirmed.
  • Agents: name, description, model, readonly. Whether Cursor accepts our model: sonnet values is unconfirmed.
  • Hooks: {"version": 1, "hooks": {"<event>": [{"command": ...}]}}, user file ~/.cursor/hooks.json, ${CURSOR_PLUGIN_ROOT} in plugin hooks. beforeShellExecution gets {command}, beforeReadFile {file_path, content}; the reply is {permission, user_message, agent_message}. permission: ask was reported broken in 2.4.21 and reads take only allow or deny.

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
1. One generated .claude-plugin/ serves Claude Code and Codex; Cursor gets .cursor-plugin/. Antigravity needs a root plugin.json; OpenCode needs a config dir plus a JS hook plugin.
  2. Commands should become skills, or be generated per harness: Codex skips $ARGUMENTS commands and Antigravity has no commands.
  3. Rules and pack extensions need rendering outside the checkout ($BRAINRC_HOME), then each harness loads them its own way. Codex plugins have no rules route yet.
  4. Guard hooks need a deny fallback: only Claude Code reliably supports ask.

docs.title: Proposed order for #50
docs.text:
1. Render to $BRAINRC_HOME; spec-agent reads extensions from there (every harness needs it).
  2. Codex through the existing .claude-plugin/: test the install, convert commands to skills.
  3. Antigravity plugin: root plugin.json, rule triggers (done, unverified); hooks after a live test.
  4. OpenCode: agent transform (#19, done); guard plugin (deny only) done in 0.3.25.
  5. Cursor: .cursor-plugin/ plugin and guard hooks (deny only) done in 0.3.26; unverified in a real Cursor.
  6. Installable brainrc (uv tool install or pipx install, from GitHub and later PyPI, core bundled): done in 0.3.22. Packs by git URL, fetched by brainrc (git + ref, brainrc update): done in 0.3.23.

docs.title: Hook latency and a native guard
docs.text: The roadmap allows native hooks only on evidence (#299). This is the evidence, measured against the owner's bar: if a tool call's p95 hook latency is over about 50 ms, port the guard evaluator to Go; if it's under, stay in Python. A full rewrite is off the table either way.

docs.title: How it was measured
docs.text:
scripts/hook_latency.py runs the hooks each tool call fires the way the tool runs them: the command from overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json through sh -c, a fresh python3 per hook, and the matching hooks of one Claude Code call in parallel. The hook-latency workflow ran it with 100 runs per case (after 3 warm-ups) on GitHub's runners, Python 3.12, three times on 2026-11-16. Session start includes E28's MCP pin check, with one pinned local stdio server.

Median / p95 in ms. Linux is ubuntu-latest (x86_64), the steadiest of its three runs; macOS is macos-latest (arm64), one column per run, because the runs disagree.

Call Hooks Linux macOS run 1 macOS run 2 macOS run 3 Baseline: sh + python3 -c pass 0 7.9 / 8.1 27.6 / 52.4 24.8 / 50.5 39.9 / 78.9 Claude Code, Bash 2 19.1 / 20.9 30.7 / 34.9 41.3 / 67.1 83.3 / 112.0 Claude Code, Bash pipeline 2 19.6 / 20.8 31.4 / 40.8 37.0 / 64.4 75.5 / 107.7 Claude Code, Read 1 18.6 / 19.3 28.5 / 29.9 37.5 / 61.2 67.7 / 110.8 Claude Code, Edit 1 19.2 / 19.9 28.6 / 32.0 41.3 / 66.4 70.8 / 96.2 Claude Code, MCP tool 1 15.7 / 16.5 26.0 / 28.1 41.1 / 69.5 48.9 / 87.8 Cursor, shell command 2 56.7 / 58.8 79.4 / 96.8 108.3 / 167.4 172.8 / 225.6 Cursor, file read 1 38.8 / 43.5 56.0 / 69.3 77.0 / 124.7 142.8 / 210.5 Session start, no pins (once) 1 26.2 / 28.0 35.5 / 36.8 48.7 / 77.0 78.4 / 105.1 Session start, 1 pinned server (once) 1 38.7 / 50.7 69.0 / 79.8 74.6 / 97.7 107.8 / 139.8

Across Linux's three runs, a Claude Code call's p95 stayed between 16 and 27 ms. Rerun with python3 scripts/hook_latency.py, or the workflow on a pull request that touches the hooks.

docs.title: Against the 50 ms bar
docs.text:
• Linux: under. A Claude Code call's p95 is at most 27 ms in every run. About 8 ms of it is starting Python; the guard work is the rest.
  • macOS: over in two of three runs. A Claude Code call's p95 was 28 to 41 ms in the first run, 61 to 70 ms in the second and 88 to 112 ms in the third.
  • Cursor: over everywhere, because its guard.py starts a second Python for each guard.
  • On macOS, most of the time is starting the interpreter, not the guard logic: an empty python3 -c pass alone had a p95 of 50 to 79 ms on those runners. The runners are shared VMs, so a developer's own Mac is likely faster, but these numbers are the evidence on hand.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
By the bar, macOS is over, so port the guard evaluator to Go, and nothing else. For the port to help, the hook a tool runs has to be the Go binary itself: a Python hook that calls a Go evaluator still pays for starting Python, which is most of the time measured here. The cheap Cursor fix (its guards in one process) is worth doing either way.

No Go work has started; it waits for the owner's go-ahead.

docs.title: Install and sync (brainrc)
docs.text:
brainrc is one Git repo of AI coding-assistant configuration (skills, agents, slash commands, rules, hooks, and MCP servers), written once and synced into Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity CLI, and Cursor by brainrc. Skills reach every harness. Rules, commands, and agents reach only some so far. Guard hooks run in Claude Code, OpenCode, and Cursor (deny only in the last two), and MCP servers sync to Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. Details per harness: harness support.

To use brainrc without editing it, install without a clone. Clone it when you want to change the config itself.

docs.title: Install with a clone
docs.text:
git clone <this-repo> ~/brainrc
cd ~/brainrc
python3 scripts/brainrc.py init     # first run: pick harnesses, bring in your CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md
python3 scripts/brainrc.py status   # dry run: shows what would be linked
python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply    # render rules + create symlinks

init asks which installed harnesses to manage and writes the answer to harnesses.local.toml. If you already have an instructions file of your own (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, ...), apply would report it as a CONFLICT, so init copies its text into rules/adopted-<harness>.local.md and moves the original aside as <file>.bak-brainrc-<time>. Adopted text is a local rule, so every harness loads it.

Run from a project folder, init also finds its CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Cursor rules and Copilot instructions and offers to import them into a pack named imported (brainrc import, packs), which every session then loads; it answers no unless you say yes, or pass --import. It skips your home folder, a brainrc checkout and links to what brainrc renders, and it writes and checks that pack before anything else, so a pack that fails leaves the rest unwritten. Then, when brainrc.local.toml sets no profile yet, it asks for a starter profile, which it writes there (below):

Starter Profile Leaves out minimal minimal: rules only everything but rules app (the default) recommended: plus skills, agents, commands and hooks MCP servers, and Gatework's Terraform, AWS, Kubernetes and GitOps skills infra full: everything nothing

Before it writes anything, init shows how many files it will create, change and move aside, how many hooks the next apply installs, and about how many tokens of rules and descriptions every session will load, then asks to go on. --yes takes the defaults without asking (no import, no starter), --harness claude,codex names the harnesses, --starter app or --profile recommended picks the profile, --no-adopt leaves your files where they are, and --dry-run writes nothing. init never runs apply.

--help lists the commands, and <command> --help shows one command's options. status and apply take --only <harness> (repeat it, or --only claude,codex) to touch only those harnesses and leave the others exactly as they are.

apply only touches harnesses that are installed, so a machine with just Claude Code gets only ~/.claude changes. A harness counts as installed when its config directory exists (~/.claude, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.gemini/config, ~/.cursor). The others are named in the output and skipped; enabled = true for one in harnesses.local.toml manages it anyway. apply records what it manages in $BRAINRC_HOME/harnesses.json.

Each harness's own variable moves its paths: $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR for Claude Code (including its .claude.json), $CODEX_HOME for Codex, and $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode for OpenCode. status, apply, doctor and uninstall read the variable when it holds an absolute path and use the default above when it is unset, empty or relative, so run them with the same environment as the harness. If the variable changes between applies, apply and status warn that brainrc's links stay in the old dir, and doctor warns while they are there. uninstall also cleans each harness's default dir, so it removes them unless the old dir was another value of the variable.

Skills, agents, commands, and hooks are symlinked from each harness back into this repo, so git pull updates them in every harness at once. To stay on a release instead of main, check out its tag (git checkout v<X.Y.Z>, from Releases) and re-run apply. Rules are different: they are rendered into ~/.config/brainrc/instructions.md ($BRAINRC_HOME to change it; $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/brainrc when that is set), so re-run apply after any change to rules/ (edits included), and after you add or remove skills, agents, or commands. For Claude Code, apply also merges the guard hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json (your other hooks are kept; a backup is written first, and the last 5 backups are kept).

docs.title: Install without a clone
docs.text:
brainrc also installs as a command from PyPI, with core's rules and hooks bundled (apply fetches Gatework, the default pack). uv fetches a Python 3.11+ if the machine has none:

uvx brainrc status          # try it without installing: a dry run that writes nothing
uv tool install brainrc     # or: pipx install brainrc
brainrc init
brainrc status
brainrc apply

With Homebrew, brew install brainrc/tap/brainrc installs the latest release from the brainrc/homebrew-tap tap; brew upgrade brainrc moves it on.

From Node, npx github:brainrc/brainrc status runs brainrc at the version in the repo's VERSION through uvx, so it needs uv but no Python; without uv it says how to get it. brainrc is not on npm: npx installs the repo itself. Keep the github:: npx brainrc would run whatever someone else publishes to npm under that name. npx may reuse a copy it fetched before, so pin a release that ships the shim with npx github:brainrc/brainrc#v<X.Y.Z>. Like uvx, it suits status and other one-off runs; install the command for apply.

CI times each of these routes from scratch to the first brainrc status on Linux and macOS, and fails one that takes over 60 seconds (scripts/check_install_time.py, workflow install-time). Homebrew, which installs Python first and whose time swings with the runner, warns over 90 seconds and fails over 180, or when its install breaks.

Pin a release with uv tool install brainrc==<X.Y.Z> (pipx install brainrc==<X.Y.Z>, uvx brainrc@<X.Y.Z>). Run apply from the installed command, not uvx: links point into the package, and uvx runs it from a cache that uv may clear. If brainrc isn't found after the install, run uv tool update-shell (or pipx ensurepath) and open a new shell. Releases from before PyPI publishing, and commits between releases, install from git: uv tool install git+https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc@v<X.Y.Z> (0.4.0 or later installs as brainrc).

Already have the old ai-config package installed? Run uv tool uninstall ai-config (or pipx uninstall ai-config): its aicfg command is outdated and works on the old settings home. The aicfg command was removed in 0.5.0: use brainrc.

Links then point into the installed package, so uv tool upgrade brainrc (or pipx upgrade brainrc) updates every harness. Guard hooks are the exception: apply copies them to $BRAINRC_HOME/hooks/core/ and links there, because the package path changes when an upgrade moves the tool to a new Python. Run brainrc apply after upgrading to refresh the copy. After an upgrade to a new Python, the other links (skills, agents) point at the old path and apply reports them as CONFLICT; brainrc apply --repair relinks them (it does the same after you move a checkout). Homebrew keeps each version under its own path, so after brew upgrade brainrc run brainrc apply --repair. Local files go in ~/.config/brainrc/ ($BRAINRC_HOME): harnesses.local.toml, packs.local.toml, and rules/*.local.md. Packs are local directories or git URLs that brainrc fetches (packs).

Upgrading from the legacy ~/.config/ai-config/ (or $AICFG_HOME)? 0.5.0 no longer reads them, and init, status, apply and update refuse (writing nothing) until you migrate. Run brainrc migrate --dry-run to see the move, then brainrc migrate: it moves the directory and re-runs apply. With the old AICFG_HOME set, set BRAINRC_HOME to the new location first.

plugin needs a checkout. Contributors use the clone above.

brainrc never overwrites a file it doesn't manage. Pre-existing files show up as CONFLICT for you to move into the repo or delete (init does that for instruction files).

Something missing in a harness? python3 scripts/brainrc.py doctor checks the install without changing anything: stale rules, missing or broken links (after moving the repo, say), broken packs, and unmerged hooks. Each problem comes with its fix. apply --repair relinks the links a moved checkout left broken, and brainrc uninstall takes out everything apply put in (--dry-run first to see it); troubleshooting.md has the details and covers the rest.

docs.title: Plugins (no clone)
docs.text: There are two plugins: brainrc (this repo) carries core's guard hooks and rules, and gatework (brainrc/gatework) carries the skills (including /brainrc-work) and the agents. Install both for what brainrc installs, minus the rules where a harness's plugins can't load them.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
/plugin marketplace add brainrc/brainrc
/plugin install brainrc@brainrc
/plugin marketplace add brainrc/gatework
/plugin install gatework@gatework
Piece Plugins brainrc Skills, agents gatework, named gatework:<name> (/gatework:brainrc-work) yes Claude guard hooks brainrc yes Rules (rules/) no: plugins can't load instructions into every session yes Packs, other harnesses (Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity, Cursor) no yes

Use one path, not both: together they load every skill and hook twice. For rules with the plugins, copy rules/*.md into your own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
codex plugin marketplace add brainrc/brainrc
codex plugin add brainrc@brainrc
codex plugin marketplace add brainrc/gatework
codex plugin add gatework@gatework

Codex gets Gatework's skills (brainrc-work, brainrc-review, brainrc-gatework-*, and the rest) and the agent files spec-agent reads. Rules don't come with a Codex plugin: run brainrc, or copy rules/*.md into ~/.codex/AGENTS.md. Whether Codex runs the brainrc plugin's guard hooks is not yet verified (harness packages).

docs.title: Antigravity CLI
docs.text:
Antigravity CLI (agy) installs each repo as a plugin from its root plugin.json:

agy plugin install https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc
agy plugin install https://github.com/brainrc/gatework

The first gets the rules: each rules/*.md carries trigger: always_on, which Antigravity needs to load it. The second gets the skills from Gatework's root skills/. Antigravity has no manifest path for agents, so the role files reach it only as files the brainrc-gatework skill reads. Guard hooks aren't included yet, so use agy's own permission settings. This install was built from Antigravity's public docs and issues and hasn't been run end to end (harness packages).

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
Cursor loads a checkout as a local plugin from .cursor-plugin/:

ln -s ~/src/brainrc ~/.cursor/plugins/local/brainrc
ln -s ~/src/gatework ~/.cursor/plugins/local/gatework

The first gets the rules (each carries alwaysApply: true) and the guard hooks for shell commands and file reads, which deny instead of asking; the second gets the skills and the agents. Use the plugins or brainrc's Cursor links, not both: brainrc links the same skills and hooks (Cursor has no user rules file, so rules come only with the plugin). Built from Cursor's official plugin repo and not yet run in a real Cursor (harness packages).

docs.title: Moving from ai-config
docs.text:
The plugin was renamed from the old ai-config to brainrc, and its skills from the old ai-config:<name> to brainrc:<name>. Remove the old one first, or every skill and hook loads twice:

  • Claude Code: /plugin uninstall ai-config@ai-config, then /plugin marketplace remove ai-config.
  • Codex: uninstall ai-config@ai-config and remove its marketplace, per Codex's docs.
  • Cursor: delete the old link ~/.cursor/plugins/local/ai-config.

Then install brainrc@brainrc as above. doctor warns until the old plugin is gone.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: macOS and Linux. Everything installs by symlink, and spec-agent reads its role files through Gatework's skills/brainrc-gatework/roles symlink, so checkouts need symlinks too. On Windows, use WSL, or turn on Developer Mode and run git config --global core.symlinks true before cloning. validate and doctor report a checkout without symlinks, with the fix.

docs.title: Per-machine customization (never committed)
docs.text:
File Purpose harnesses.local.toml Disable a harness ([cursor] / enabled = false), manage one that isn't detected (enabled = true), or change paths packs.local.toml Layer extra repos on top: skills, agents, rules, hooks, spec-agent extensions (packs.md); [gatework] enabled = false drops the default pack brainrc.local.toml What this machine installs: profile and exclude (below) rules/*.local.md Private rules appended after the shared ones

brainrc.local.toml picks a profile (brainrc init --profile <name> writes it) and drops items by path:

profile = "recommended"   # minimal: rules only; recommended: plus skills, agents, commands
                          # and hooks; full (the default): plus MCP servers
exclude = ["skills/brainrc-aws", "gatework:agents/brainrc-infra-*"]   # fnmatch, per source

A pattern matches an item's path in its source (skills/brainrc-aws), or that path after the pack's name (gatework:skills/brainrc-aws). apply prunes what a profile or pattern drops; validate still checks everything.

Content that must never live in this repo (an employer's facts and skills, for example) goes in a pack: a separate repo with the same layout. See packs.md. python3 scripts/brainrc.py tokens shows what each skill, agent, and rule costs in context.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
rules/          Global instructions, as ordered markdown fragments (00-core.md, 10-git.md, ...).
                Concatenated into CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md.
commands/       Optional, for packs: slash commands. Gatework's (/brainrc-work, /brainrc-review, /brainrc-gatework-*) are skills.
mcp/            Canonical MCP server registry. Env var names only, never secret values.
overrides/      Harness-specific config (Claude guard hooks + settings fragment).
harnesses.toml  Where each harness reads each content type.
packs.toml      The default pack, Gatework (brainrc/gatework, fetched by `apply`); extra source
                repos ("packs") go in packs.local.toml.
VERSION         Core version that packs pin with `requires_core`; changes in CHANGELOG.md.
changelog.d/    One fragment per unreleased change; folded into CHANGELOG.md on release.
brainrc/        The brainrc package: sync, validate, doctor, plugin, tokens (Python 3.11+, stdlib only).
scripts/        brainrc.py (runs the package), evals.py, release.py.
docs/           spec-agent, guardrails, efficiency, formats, troubleshooting, harness packages, roadmap.
tests/          stdlib unittest for brainrc and hooks.
examples/       Sandbox project + tickets for trying spec-agent.
dist/           Generated output (gitignored).

docs.title: Packs
docs.text:
A pack is a separate repo layered on top of this one. Use it for content that must not live here: an employer's facts, internal skills, private review rules. This repo stays generic, and each machine picks the packs it needs.

To start one, copy the working example in examples/pack-acme. For a pack with a guard hook, see examples/pack-homelab. Or start from the instructions you already have: brainrc import turns them into a pack (Import).

docs.title: Enable a pack
docs.text:
List it in packs.local.toml (gitignored; for an installed brainrc, in ~/.config/brainrc/), then apply:

[acme]
path = "~/src/acme-ai-pack"   # ~ and $VARS expand; relative paths are relative to this file
# enabled = false             # removes the pack's links and hooks on the next apply

python3 scripts/brainrc.py status   # dry run
python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply

Or name it by git URL and let brainrc fetch it, with no clone of your own:

[acme]
git = "git@github.com:acme/acme-ai-pack.git"   # any URL git accepts; private repos use your git credentials
ref = "v1.2.0"                                 # tag, branch, or commit; default: the remote's default branch

apply fetches it (shallow, detached) into ~/.config/brainrc/packs/acme and records the URL and ref it fetched; after that it works offline. Change ref or git and the next apply fetches again (status shows the FETCH line first). apply records the commit each ref resolved to, and a hash of every file it installed, in ~/.config/brainrc/brainrc.lock, and from then on keeps the pack at that commit, even when the tag or branch moves. brainrc update [<pack> ...] (or python3 scripts/brainrc.py update) moves the pin: it refetches the packs at their ref, prints the commits and installed files that change, then applies (pinned commits). Both refuse a clone with local changes, and stop any git call after 60s. Pin a tag, and bump ref to upgrade. doctor reports a git pack that hasn't been fetched yet or whose clone doesn't match its git and ref.

The lock also records what each pack can do: its hooks, MCP servers, tool grants and network domains. status lists any added (PERMS ... +) or removed, and apply asks before adding any unless you pass --yes (permissions).

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
brainrc import PATH ... writes the instruction files you already have as a pack, so they move over in one command. A folder means the files in it that brainrc reads.

Source Becomes CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md one rule per section, in order Cursor: .cursor/rules/**/*.mdc, .cursorrules alwaysApply: true rules and .cursorrules become rules; a rule scoped by globs becomes a skill with a row in Gatework's Domains table for those globs; one with only a description becomes a skill with that description Copilot: .github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md copilot-instructions.md becomes one rule per section; a path-specific file with applyTo: "**" becomes a rule, one scoped to other globs a skill with a Domains row, one with neither a skill loaded on request, as for Cursor; one for code review only (excludeAgent: coding-agent) is skipped

Each file is split at the shallowest heading level it uses more than once (a lone # Title stays with the text under it), and each part becomes rules/NN-<heading>.md with a first-line comment naming the file and lines it came from. Headings inside code blocks don't count. A CLAUDE.md line that is only @path (Claude Code's import) is replaced by that file's rules, and a brainrc project block is left out, since install writes it.

brainrc import ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md --name mine --enable   # write ~/.config/brainrc/imported/mine, load it
brainrc import . --to tools/agent-pack --dry-run          # what a repo's files would become

The pack goes to $BRAINRC_HOME/imported/<name> unless --to names a folder, and is checked as validate --pack would. import never overwrites a folder with files in it; --force replaces an earlier pack there (a folder with a pack.toml), never one that holds a source. --enable adds it to packs.local.toml; for one project, list it in brainrc.toml instead (project).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Same as this repo. Every folder is optional.

acme-ai-pack/
  pack.toml              name, prefix, extensions for other packs (see Extensions)
  validator.py           optional checks and renders of its own (see Validator plugins)
  tests/                 the pack's own tests, which validate --pack runs (see Pack tests)
  skills/acme-*/         linked next to the core skills
  agents/acme-*.md       linked next to the core agents
  commands/acme-*.md
  rules/NN-*.md          rendered after all core rules, as one labelled block (see Rules)
  overrides/claude/hooks/                 linked to <hooks_dir>-acme (e.g. ~/.claude/hooks/brainrc-acme)
  overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json merged after the core fragment; {{hooks_dir}} = the pack's hooks dir
  overrides/opencode/plugin.js            linked beside core's guard plugin, as brainrc-guard-acme.js
  mcp/servers.toml       MCP servers, synced after core's (see formats.md#mcp-servers-mcpserverstoml)
  tripwires.toml         patterns that must not appear in the pack (checked by validate)

Skills, agents, commands, and MCP servers must start with the pack's prefix, and no name may exist in two sources. apply refuses to write anything if one does. The full rules are in Naming.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
A clear name is the cheapest trust signal a pack has. Every pack follows these seven rules:

  1. brainrc- and brainrc/ are reserved for official packs. No other pack's name, prefix or ID starts with them.
  2. A registry prefix starts with the owner's handle. A pack published as jdoe/k8s-tools uses a prefix such as jdoe- or jdoe-k8s-.
  3. No vendor names without verification. A pack's name, prefix and ID don't use a vendor's name (aws, github, openai and the like) unless the vendor itself is verified as its owner.
  4. No names one or two edits from an official name. The official names are brainrc and the IDs in the table below, so brainrx- and brianrc/review are refused.
  5. ASCII lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only, in names, prefixes, IDs and item names.
  6. A prefix is 2 to 24 characters, not counting its trailing hyphen.
  7. Item names are prefix-scoped. Every skill, agent, command and MCP server starts with the pack's prefix, so two packs' items can't collide.

validate and apply refuse a pack that breaks one. The vendor names and the official IDs it checks are listed in brainrc/naming.py.

A pack's ID is <owner>/<pack>, where the owner is the GitHub user or organization that publishes it. Official packs are owned by brainrc:

ID What it holds Issue brainrc/gatework the default pack: spec-agent, its roles, ticket connectors and domain skills (brainrc/gatework) #172 brainrc/starter the small, measured base for the default profile #313 brainrc/review review, PR description, commit message and unslop #314 brainrc/go Go, built from today's brainrc-go-service skill #315 brainrc/terraform-aws Terraform and AWS #316 brainrc/kubernetes Kubernetes, including GitOps #317 brainrc/security-baseline the default guard policy, secret protection and a sandbox profile #323

docs.title: pack.toml
docs.text:
name = "acme"
prefix = "acme-"          # default: "<name>-"
id = "acme/acme-ai-pack"  # optional: the <owner>/<pack> ID it's published under (see Naming)
requires_core = ">=0.7, <0.9"   # core versions this pack works with (see Compatibility)
max_always_tokens = 800   # optional budget for rules + descriptions (see Context cost)
test = "tests"            # optional: tests validate --pack runs (see Pack tests)

[extensions.gatework]      # what the gatework pack (spec-agent) reads; see Extensions
deliver_checks = [        # listed in the Deliver gate as done / not applicable / not run
  "Deploy plan reviewed by the owning team",
]

[[extensions.gatework.domains]]   # extra rows for spec-agent's Domains table
files = "`deploy/*.yaml`, `charts/acme-*`"
skills = ["acme-deploy"]
reviewer = "brainrc-infra-reviewer"

[[extensions.gatework.intake_context]]   # skills spec-agent runs after fetching the ticket
skill = "acme-context"
when = "every ticket"

[extensions.gatework.ticket]   # a connector for this pack's ticket refs, with its config
connector = "brainrc-ticket-jira"
refs = ["ACME-*"]
host = "acme.example.net"
blocked_status = "Blocked"
instructions = "Link the PR in the ticket's Development panel."   # see Connector config

validate checks pack.toml against schemas/pack.toml.schema.json: a known key with a value of the wrong type fails, and a key it doesn't know warns, naming the closest known key (max_always_token → max_always_tokens), since brainrc would otherwise ignore it. Only validate reports these; apply still installs the pack.

docs.title: Editor completion
docs.text:
A pack's pack.toml and mcp/servers.toml have JSON Schemas in docs/schemas/ (pack.toml, mcp-servers.toml), as does core's harnesses.toml. Editors that use Taplo (VS Code's Even Better TOML, Zed, Helix) complete keys and flag wrong ones from a first line naming the schema, which brainrc import writes for you:

#:schema https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brainrc/brainrc/main/docs/schemas/pack.toml.schema.json
name = "acme"

In a checkout of this repo, .taplo.toml maps each file to its schema. Files outside it (a pack's own repo, ~/.config/brainrc/harnesses.local.toml) take the #:schema line.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
[extensions.<namespace>] is a table another pack reads; core passes it through untouched. The pack that owns the namespace checks it with its validator plugin, and validate warns about a table no enabled pack reads. Gatework, the default pack, owns [extensions.gatework] above. apply renders every enabled pack's table into $BRAINRC_HOME/extensions.md (default ~/.config/brainrc/extensions.md), which spec-agent reads at intake. With no other packs enabled, the file says so and spec-agent runs as before; with Gatework disabled, there is no file.

The forms from before 0.7.0, the same keys directly under [extensions] or under [extensions.spec-agent], still work and warn until 0.8.0: move them under [extensions.gatework]. apply no longer writes the old copy at skills/spec-agent/references/extensions.md, and removes it.

A pack has at most one [extensions.ticket]: one connector and the refs it handles. A team with two ticket systems splits them into two packs. The connector, core or the pack's own, must follow the connector contract, which validate checks.

docs.title: Connector config
docs.text:
A connector skill declares the keys its table takes, and their types, in its SKILL.md frontmatter under the Agent Skills metadata map, so every harness still loads it:

---
name: acme-ticket-desk
description: Ticket connector for the Acme service desk. Use for DESK- refs.
metadata:
  brainrc-config: "refs: list required; queue: integer; blocked_status: string"
---

Each key: type entry is one of string, integer, boolean or list (of strings), followed by required when the table must set it. validate then checks every pack table that names the skill as its connector: a key of the wrong type or a missing required key fails, and a key the connector doesn't declare warns. Only validate reports these; apply still installs the pack. A connector that declares nothing, or a declaration with a mistake (which fails on the skill), isn't checked. Every table may also set instructions: what the pack tells the connector about its tickets, in place of free-form keys such as notes. It reaches the model, so the pack's tripwires check it like the pack's other text, unless a tripwire sets paths or excludes pack.toml.

docs.title: Validator plugins
docs.text:
A pack can check what only it understands: validator = "validator.py" in pack.toml names a Python module in the pack. Each name in it is optional:

Name What core does with it NAMESPACE the [extensions.<namespace>] table it owns (default: the pack's name) LEGACY_KEYS, LEGACY_NAMESPACES, REMOVED_IN older extension forms it still reads; validate warns until REMOVED_IN check_extensions(table, where, skill_names, agent_names) errors in one pack's table, before apply writes anything warn_extensions(table, where) warnings for one pack's table, from validate check(me, sources) errors across every source, from validate doctor(me) (FAIL or WARN, what, fix) findings for doctor render_extensions(tables) the text of $BRAINRC_HOME/extensions.md

A validator is the pack's code running inside brainrc, so core runs it only for a default pack (core's packs.toml pins it, or your own packs.local.toml points it elsewhere), for the pack validate --pack checks, and for a pack whose entry in packs.local.toml sets run_validator = true. Otherwise validate warns that the pack ships one. Gatework's validator.py is the reference.

docs.title: Pack tests
docs.text:
test = "tests" in pack.toml names the pack's own unittest tests: a directory (its test*.py files) or one .py file. validate --pack runs them in a fresh Python, from the pack's root, and fails if one fails or none is found. They are the pack's code, so only validate --pack from the command line runs them; doctor and apply never do.

brainrc.testing runs a guard hook the way Claude Code does, a PreToolUse payload on stdin, so a test needs no scaffolding of its own. A string is a Bash command; a dict is the whole payload:

from brainrc.testing import assert_allows, assert_asks, assert_denies, assert_no_opinion, run_hook

HOOK = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "overrides/claude/hooks/guard_acme.py"

class GuardTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_asks_before_a_deploy(self):
        assert_asks(HOOK, "acme deploy prod")      # the risky command
        assert_allows(HOOK, "acme deploy --help")  # and a safe near-miss

assert_allows passes when the hook allows or has no opinion, and assert_no_opinion only when it stays out, so Claude Code's own permission check still decides; assert_denies counts exit code 2 as a deny. Each lists every case that came out wrong, and a missing, failing or hung hook fails. run_hook(hook, payload) returns the decision itself. pack-homelab has a full example.

docs.title: Default packs
docs.text:
A default pack is a table in core's shipped packs.toml: core turns it on unless packs.local.toml says otherwise. Gatework is the only one: spec-agent (the brainrc-gatework skill), its roles, the ticket connectors and the domain skills. It lives in brainrc/gatework, and packs.toml pins it by git and a release tag ref, so apply fetches it like any git pack (update refetches). Before 0.7.1 it shipped inside core as packs/gatework.

Its names before 0.7.0 (spec-agent, spec-status, ticket-github, kubernetes and the rest, listed in brainrc/naming.py) are deprecated aliases until 0.8.0, and the only names naming rule 7 lets it keep without its prefix. [gatework] with enabled = false in packs.local.toml turns it off (brainrc init asks), and core then installs its rules and guard hooks and nothing else. To try another version, set only ref there; to work on a clone, set path, which replaces the shipped git and ref:

[gatework]
path = "~/src/gatework"

validate --pack checks a pack against core and the default packs on disk, so a pack that extends Gatework is checked against it once apply has fetched it; until then validate warns that it isn't fetched yet. --fetch-defaults fetches them at the versions core pins instead (see Validate a pack in its own CI).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
The rendered instructions file has three parts, in this order:

  1. Core rules, in filename order.
  2. Each enabled pack's rules, one block per pack in packs.toml order, filename order inside. Each block starts with <!-- pack: <name> --> and a line telling the model the rules refine the ones above.
  3. *.local.md rules from any source, under <!-- local -->.

Pack rule numbers only order rules within the pack. Later rules refine earlier ones and must not contradict them: a pack rule that contradicts core is a bug in the pack. Write it as a narrower case ("in Acme repos, also ...") instead.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Core's version is in VERSION. CHANGELOG.md tags changes that affect packs with [pack contract]. Declare the versions your pack supports with requires_core: comma-separated clauses of >=, >, <=, <, ==, != and a version (missing parts are zero, and a bare version means >=).

  • Not satisfied → validate fails and apply/status write nothing, naming the pack.
  • Missing → allowed, with a warning.
  • Policy: semver. While core is 0.x, a breaking pack-contract change bumps MINOR, so pin ">=0.N, <0.N+1". After 1.0, breaking changes bump MAJOR: pin ">=1.N, <2". Other changes (new skills, fixes, docs) bump PATCH and never break a pin.

docs.title: tripwires.toml
docs.text:
Stale facts that must not come back, checked by validate:

[[tripwire]]
id = "old-pager"
pattern = '(?i)\bpagerbot\b'
message = "pagerbot was replaced by the new on-call tool"
allow = '(?i)replaced|decommissioned|never'   # lines matching this pass (they warn against it)
paths = ["*.md"]                              # default; fnmatch against the path in the pack

docs.title: Validate a pack in its own CI
docs.text:
The validate-pack action checks a pack against the core version you pin, and against core's default packs (Gatework) at the versions that core pins, so a pack may use their skills and agents:

- uses: actions/checkout@<sha>
- uses: brainrc/brainrc/.github/actions/validate-pack@<core tag or sha>
  with:
    path: .                  # the pack's directory (default: the repository root)
    # default-packs: "false" checks it against core alone
    # python-version: "3.12" sets one up; by default it uses the python3 on PATH

The ref you pin is the core: GitHub runs the action from that commit of this repository, so there is nothing else to clone. To check before each commit, add the pre-commit hook, which installs brainrc at the rev you pin:

- repo: https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc
  rev: <core tag>
  hooks:
    - id: brainrc-validate-pack
      # args: [pack]          # the pack's directory, when it isn't the repository root

Both run validate --pack <dir> --fetch-defaults, which fetches the default packs at the refs core's packs.toml pins into clones of their own under $BRAINRC_HOME/validate-packs/ (once; later runs reuse them), never the clones apply links.

Without either, clone core at the version you pin and run it yourself:

git clone --depth 1 --branch <core tag> https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc core
python3 core/scripts/brainrc.py validate --pack . --fetch-defaults

This checks the core, the default packs on disk and that pack, whatever else is in packs.toml: frontmatter; pack.toml against its schema; cross-references in skills, agents, commands, rules, README.md and docs/** (relative links, [agent: x] tags, and skills named as "x skill" or in prose as "the x skill"; pack files may reference core's and Gatework's skills and agents); the naming rules; collisions; extension references and connector config; requires_core; tripwires; and the pack's own tests. A skill named in prose counts only when its name has a hyphen and starts with the pack's prefix or a first part two known skills share, so "the follow-up skill" stays prose. A relative link in a rule warns, since rules are rendered into each harness's own file; link a URL. apply refuses a pack only for what would break the install (frontmatter, names, collisions, tags, links in skills, agents and commands); the rest only validate reports.

docs.title: Packs and Claude Code plugins
docs.text: Core also ships as a Claude Code plugin (README, Install). Packs stay brainrc packs: a plugin could carry a pack's skills, agents, and hooks, but not its rules or its spec-agent extensions (domains, ticket connector, Deliver checks), which brainrc apply renders for Gatework. Revisit if plugins gain a way to extend another plugin.

docs.title: Context cost
docs.text:
python3 scripts/brainrc.py tokens estimates tokens per skill, agent, and command across all enabled sources. It also shows what loads in every session (rules and descriptions) versus on use. Keep pack rules short: they load in every session on that machine.

validate enforces a budget on each source's always-loaded tokens (its rules plus its skill, agent, and command descriptions). Core's is 3,000. A pack declares its own in pack.toml:

max_always_tokens = 800

Over a declared budget, validate fails and names the biggest items. A pack without max_always_tokens gets a warning above 1,000 tokens. Any description over 100 tokens gets a warning: say what the skill does and when to use it, and move the rest into the body.

docs.title: Post-deliver: following a PR to merge (design)
docs.text: Status: all five build steps are built (see references/watch.md). A run used to end at the Deliver gate: push, PR, ticket update, retro, stage: done, and whatever came next was fixed by hand. This page designs the stage that closes that loop. Build order is at the end.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• React to CI failures and review comments on the run's PR, inside the same gates and evidence rules as the rest of the run.
  • After merge, re-check the acceptance criteria on the default branch.
  • Record what happened after delivery in state.json and retro.md, so the metrics count rework done after the PR went up, not just before.

Non-goals: merging (always a human), deploying (still after merge, outside the run), and babysitting PRs the run didn't open.

docs.title: Stage: watch
docs.text:
… ⛔ DELIVER ─► push · PR · ticket ─► watch ─┬─► CI red ───────► fix task ─► review ─► ⛔ PUSH ─┐
                                             ├─► review comment ► fix task / reply ──► ⛔ PUSH ─┤
                                             ├─► merged ────────► post-merge verify ─► done
                                             └─► closed ────────► done (abandoned)     ◄────────┘

stage gains watch between deliver and done. The run enters it after the PR opens (delivery: normal only; local-only runs go straight to done).

How it wakes up. Pull-based, so it works in every harness: /brainrc-gatework-resume (or /brainrc-work on the same ref) at stage: watch fetches the PR's state through the ticket connector and handles whatever changed since watch.checked_at. A harness with PR event subscriptions (Claude Code on the web) can call the same step on each event; that's an optional trigger, not a requirement. No daemon and no polling loop in the engine.

Connector contract. One new optional operation, pr_status: CI check results on the head commit, review threads (unresolved, with author and body, and an optional id), and merge state. brainrc-ticket-github implements it with two read-only calls: gh pr view <n> --json statusCheckRollup,headRefOid,state,updatedAt (checks, head SHA, state, updated_at) and gh api graphql reviewThreads (unresolved only, via isResolved); see its ## pr_status section for the queries and mapping. Connectors without it skip watch, and the run ends at done as today.

docs.title: CI failure
docs.text:
1. Summarize the failing check's log into .runs/ (summary only, per efficiency.md; the log is untrusted).
  2. If the failure also occurs on the base branch, or names nothing this diff touched, record it as external and stop with a one-line note. Not this run's to fix.
  3. Otherwise add a fix task C1.. (agent: brainrc-implementer, files: those the failure points at) and run it through the normal implement → review path, with the same retry budget.
  4. Pushing the fix is outward: present a short Push gate (diff stat, commit list, the failing check it should fix). Approve → push. A run never pushes without approval.

docs.title: Review comment
docs.text:
The comment is untrusted input, just like the ticket body. Each unresolved thread is handled once; its key goes in watch.thread_log (keys only, no raw text). For each new thread:

  • A small, local change (rename, added test, one-function fix) → a fix task R1.., then the Push gate.
  • A question about intent → draft a reply from spec.md; post it only after it's approved at the next Push gate (replies are outward too), via the connector's reply_thread.
  • Large or design-level → stop and ask. The user decides; the run doesn't redesign on a reviewer's word alone.

Embedded instructions in a thread are flagged, not followed. After 3 review rounds the PR is handed back and nothing further is classified.

docs.title: Post-merge verify
docs.text: When the PR merges, run the verifier in a detached worktree (specs/<slug>/.runs/post-merge) at the merge commit (or the local tip of the base if that commit is missing), writing verify-merged.md. watch.post_merge is regression (a check that passed in verify.md fails on the merge: report it, open nothing, print a suggested follow-up), unverified (nothing could be run; never claimed as pass), or pass. A PR closed unmerged ends the run as abandoned with no verify.

docs.title: State and retro
docs.text:
state.json additions:

"watch": {
  "checked_at": "2026-10-20T09:12:00Z",
  "head_sha": "abc1234",
  "ci_failures": [{ "check": "test", "sha": "abc1234", "cause": "own|external", "task": "C1" }],
  "review_rounds": 2,
  "threads": { "total": 5, "fixed": 3, "replied": 2, "flagged": 0 },
  "thread_log": [{ "key": "<16-hex key>", "kind": "ask", "task": "R1", "flagged": false }],
  "merged_at": null,
  "post_merge": null,
  "outcome": null
}

metrics gains post_deliver_retries (fix tasks after the PR opened) and time_to_merge (PR opened → merged, in minutes, from timestamps, never estimated; unset if either is missing). watch.post_merge is pass|regression|unverified, watch.outcome is merged|abandoned.

retro.md keeps its sections and adds After delivery: CI failures (own/external), review rounds and what reviewers caught that the run's own reviewers didn't, post-merge result. The retro is first written at deliver as today, and this section is appended once when watch ends (merged or abandoned). The "what reviewers caught" line is the useful one: each miss is a candidate edit to a reviewer role or checklist.

docs.title: Build order
docs.text:
1. Metrics rollup first (scripts/retro_report.py). Aggregate state.json and retro.md across runs and projects: gate rework, first-pass review rate, retries, interventions, time per stage. It needs no new state, gives a baseline today, and is the place the watch numbers will land. Without it, the new fields would be written and never read. Done.
  2. pr_status in the connector contract and brainrc-ticket-github; validate accepts it as optional. Done.
  3. watch stage for CI failures and the Push gate. Done.
  4. Review comments. Done.
  5. Post-merge verify and the retro's After delivery section; add them to the rollup. Done.

Each step is one PR and ships with an eval: a sandbox ticket with a fake pr_status fixture (red CI, then a review comment, then merged), graded with scripts/evals.py check.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Should the Push gate be skippable for fix-only pushes on a run's own branch? Default no: start strict and loosen with retro data.
  • After how many rounds should watch give up and hand the PR back? Proposal: the existing retry budget per fix task, plus a stop after 3 review rounds.

docs.title: Project manifest and lockfile
docs.text:
A team commits two files to its repo: brainrc.toml, which says which packs the repo's agents use, and brainrc.lock, which records exactly what those packs were when apply last ran. Every machine and CI job then produces the same agent files from the same lock.

This page is the contract for both files. It is language-neutral: another implementation that reads and writes them as described here is compatible. The JSON Schemas schemas/brainrc.toml.schema.json and schemas/brainrc.lock.schema.json describe each file after it is parsed as TOML; brainrc checks both files against them on every read. Conformance fixtures are in tests/fixtures/lockfile/.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
• User scope is what brainrc has always done: packs from packs.toml and packs.local.toml, linked into each installed harness's home. Its lock is $BRAINRC_HOME/brainrc.lock (default ~/.config/brainrc/brainrc.lock).
  • Project scope is a repo with brainrc.toml at its root. Its agent files are written into the repo, and its lock is brainrc.lock next to brainrc.toml. brainrc finds the project from the current directory: that directory or a parent, up to the repo root (the first directory that holds .git).

Both scopes apply together. The user's own config still layers on top of a project's at run time, because harnesses read the user's home and the repo.

docs.title: What apply writes in a project
docs.text:
brainrc apply (and status, which writes nothing) runs the user scope first, then the project in the current directory, under its own Project <dir> (brainrc.toml) heading.

  • Skills are copied, not linked, to .agents/skills/<name>/, so the repo works on every machine and in CI. A link inside a skill (Gatework's roles/) is copied as the files it points to.
  • Rules from the project's packs go into a marked block in AGENTS.md: <!-- brainrc:begin: … --> to <!-- brainrc:end -->. Your own text above and below the block stays. With no rules, there is no block, and a file that held only the block is removed.
  • Standard files first. Codex, OpenCode, Cursor and Antigravity read .agents/skills/ and AGENTS.md themselves, so they get nothing else. A tool that can't read them names its own places in harnesses.toml (project_skills, project_instructions). Today that is Claude Code only: skills are copied to .claude/skills/ too, and CLAUDE.md gets a marked block holding @AGENTS.md, unless it already reads AGENTS.md (a link to it, or its own @AGENTS.md line). harnesses in brainrc.toml picks which tools get their own files; drop one and its files and block are removed.
Tool Skills Instructions Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity .agents/skills/ AGENTS.md Claude Code .claude/skills/ (copy) CLAUDE.md block importing AGENTS.md
  • Only the project's packs: core's rules and guard hooks, MCP servers and anything machine-local (packs.local.toml, brainrc.local.toml, *.local.md) stay in the user scope, so they never change a project's files.
  • Git packs are fetched by apply, never by status, into $BRAINRC_HOME/project-packs/<key>-<id>, one clone per URL and ref.
  • Ownership: brainrc.lock lists every file brainrc wrote (outputs). A file there is updated or removed as its pack changes. A file brainrc didn't write, or one you changed after it was removed from the packs, is a CONFLICT and is left alone.

docs.title: Pinned commits and update
docs.text:
apply resolves each git pack's ref once and records the commit in the lock. After that the commit is pinned: apply, status and install keep the pack at the lock's commit, on this machine and on a teammate's, even when the tag is moved or the branch (or the remote's default branch, for a pack with no ref) moves on. A clone found at another commit is put back (FETCH <pack> <url> (<ref>, locked at <commit>)). Changing git or ref in the config is a deliberate move, so the next apply fetches the new ref and relocks.

brainrc update [<pack> ...] is the one command that moves a pin to what the ref resolves to now. It refetches the named packs (every git pack when none is named; in a project, the project's packs of that name too) and, before anything is relinked or relocked, prints for each pack:

MOVED     gatework  v0.7.1: 753b9960c5e0 -> 8c41d2f0a9b3  (user scope)
          commit    8c41d2f Tighten the review checklist
          added     skills/brainrc-new/SKILL.md
          changed   skills/brainrc-work/SKILL.md

The commits are the ones between the old pin and the new one (up to 50; an older pin that isn't in them is named, as a rewritten history or a longer gap), and the files are the pack's installed files whose hash changed. CURRENT says nothing moved. Then it runs apply, which relocks. A failed fetch applies nothing, and the next apply puts the pack back at its pin.

docs.title: Installing from the lock
docs.text: brainrc install --frozen installs exactly what brainrc.lock records, for CI and teammates. It fetches each git pack's locked commit, never its ref, so a moved tag changes nothing. Every check runs before anything is written: the packs in brainrc.toml (or packs.toml) and the lock must match by key, URL, ref and path, and every file must hash as the lock says, outputs included. On any mismatch it names each one, writes nothing and exits 1. It never rewrites the lock and never removes files. It won't overwrite a file brainrc didn't write either: one at a locked path whose hash is neither the lock's nor what brainrc last wrote there on this machine (kept in $BRAINRC_HOME/project-state/), or a hand-edited block in AGENTS.md. It names each one and writes nothing; --force overwrites them. Neither writes through an AGENTS.md that is a link. The scope is the project when there is a brainrc.toml here or above, else the user; --scope user|project picks one. brainrc install without --frozen is apply.

docs.title: Checking for drift in CI
docs.text:
brainrc check exits 1 when anything differs from brainrc.lock, naming each difference: a pack in brainrc.toml the lock doesn't have (or the reverse), a pack file this machine has that hashes differently, a file brainrc owns in the repo that was edited, removed or added to, and its block in AGENTS.md. It uses no network and writes nothing. A git pack not fetched on this machine is checked through the repo's files; a clone at another commit than the lock's is reported as MOVED and doesn't fail (apply puts it back).

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- name: Agent files match brainrc.lock
  run: pipx run --spec git+https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc brainrc check

brainrc install --frozen after it also fetches each git pack at its locked commit and checks it.

docs.title: brainrc.toml
docs.text:
version = 1                                  # optional; 1 is the only version
exclude = ["gatework:skills/brainrc-aws"]    # optional; items to leave out (see below)
harnesses = ["claude", "codex"]              # optional; tools that get their own files

[packs.gatework]        # a default pack: on unless `enabled = false`
ref = "v0.7.1"          # pin it to another ref; its `git` URL is kept

[packs.acme]
git = "https://example.com/acme/agent-pack.git"
ref = "v2"

[packs.team]
path = "tools/agent-pack"   # relative to the repo root
Key Type Meaning version integer Format version. 1, the default. exclude array of strings Items not to install, as a path in the pack (skills/brainrc-aws) or after its name (gatework:skills/brainrc-aws); * and ? match. harnesses array of strings Harnesses (from harnesses.toml) that get tool-specific files besides the standard ones. Default: every enabled harness in core's harnesses.toml (never harnesses.local.toml); [] for the standard files only. packs.<key> table One pack. <key> is lowercase letters, digits and -. packs.<key>.enabled boolean Default true. false turns a default pack off. packs.<key>.git string A URL to fetch. Can't start with -. packs.<key>.ref string With git: tag, branch or commit. Default: the remote's default branch. packs.<key>.path string A directory inside the repo, relative to the repo root, using /. No .., ~, $ or leading /. packs.<key>.description string A note for people; ignored.
  • Default packs are the tables in core's packs.toml (Gatework). They are on in every project unless brainrc.toml sets enabled = false. A ref alone keeps the default pack's URL; git or path replaces its origin.
  • Any other pack needs exactly one of git and path.
  • Unknown keys are errors, so a typo never silently changes what is installed.

docs.title: brainrc.lock
docs.text:
apply writes it; nobody edits it. A second apply with no change to any source leaves it byte-identical.

# brainrc.lock: written by brainrc. Don't edit it by hand.
version = 2
brainrc = "0.7.3"
scope = "project"

[packs.gatework]
git = "https://github.com/brainrc/gatework.git"
ref = "v0.7.1"
commit = "753b9960c5e0d2f1a4b7c8e9d0a1b2c3d4e5f607"

[packs.gatework.files]
"agents/brainrc-analyst.md" = "sha256:3f1c…"
"skills/brainrc-work/SKILL.md" = "sha256:9a0b…"

[packs.team]
path = "tools/agent-pack"

[packs.team.files]
"skills/team-deploy/SKILL.md" = "sha256:5d2e…"

[outputs]
".agents/skills/brainrc-work/SKILL.md" = "sha256:9a0b…"

[blocks]
"AGENTS.md" = "sha256:77c4…"
Key Type Meaning version integer Format version, 2. Version 2 adds packs.<key>.permissions; brainrc reads 1 and 2 and writes 2. A reader refuses a newer version and names the brainrc that wrote it, so brainrc 0.7.7 and older say to upgrade instead of failing on permissions. brainrc string The brainrc version that wrote it, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. scope string user or project. packs.<key> table Every enabled pack, and nothing for a disabled one. packs.<key>.git string The URL fetched, with any user name or password removed. packs.<key>.ref string The ref asked for (HEAD when the config names none). packs.<key>.commit string The commit that ref resolved to: 40 or 64 lowercase hex digits. Git packs only. packs.<key>.path string A path pack's directory as the config wrote it; under the home directory it is written with ~. Path packs have no commit. packs.<key>.files table Every installed file of the pack (below): its path in the pack, using /, to its hash. packs.<key>.permissions table What the pack can do in this scope (permissions): hooks, mcp, tools, domains, each a sorted array of strings, present only when not empty. outputs table Project scope: every file brainrc wrote into the repo, repo-relative, to its hash. blocks table Project scope: files brainrc shares with you (AGENTS.md): the hash of its marked block.

A hash is sha256: and 64 lowercase hex digits, the SHA-256 of the file's bytes. A pack has exactly one of git (with commit) and path. outputs and blocks appear only in a project lock, and only when they have entries; empty files tables are written too.

A pack's installed files are the files brainrc reads from it to install: pack.toml, the file its validator names, rules/*.md (not README.md or *.local.md), each item it installs (every file under skills/<name>/, agents/<name>.md, commands/<name>.md) after the profile and exclude are applied, and, in user scope with hooks installed, every file under overrides/. Symbolic links are followed, so a file is hashed as it is read. __pycache__ directories are skipped.

Determinism. The lock is UTF-8 with \n line endings and ends with one newline. The first line is the comment above. Then come version, brainrc and scope, in that order. Then one [packs.<key>] table per pack sorted by key, its keys in the order git, ref, commit, or path, each followed by its [packs.<key>.files] table and its [packs.<key>.permissions] table (arrays written one string per line, sorted). Then [outputs] and [blocks]. Every table's entries are sorted by key (by Unicode code point). Keys that aren't bare keys (A-Za-z0-9_-) are written as basic strings. Strings escape ", \ and control characters as TOML basic strings do. The lock holds no timestamps, no host or user names, no credentials and no absolute path to the home directory.

Ready for more. Future keys (pinned commands, more permission records) are added inside packs.<key> or as new top-level tables, with a version bump only for a change an old reader would misread.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The lock records what each pack can do in its scope, so a pack can't widen it unseen:

Field Entries hooks Each hook its overrides/<harness>/settings.fragment.json adds: <harness> <event> [<matcher>] <command>. User scope, when the profile installs hooks. Also brainrc validator <file> when pack.toml names a validator, in both scopes. mcp Each MCP server in its mcp/servers.toml: name, URL or command and arguments, the variables it reads and its harnesses. User scope, full profile. tools Each installed agent's tools (an agent without them gets (every tool)), each skill's and command's allowed-tools, the fragment's permissions (<harness> allow <rule>, deny, ask), and any other key it sets with its value (<harness> sets statusLine = {...}; a sha256 when over 200 characters). domains Each host the pack's MCP URLs and domain: grants name.

status prints PERMS <pack> + <kind> <entry> for what apply would add and - for what it would remove. apply (and update, and install without --frozen) asks before writing anything when any entry is added or a deny or ask rule is removed, and --yes accepts them. Without a terminal to ask in (CI, a script, a pipe) and without --yes, it refuses and writes nothing; there is no variable that skips the question. Removing any other entry never asks. When update is refused, the git packs it moved go back to the commits the lock pins, since the harnesses link into them.

A machine's first lock has nothing to widen from: its permissions are listed once as PERMS lines and recorded as the baseline. A pack added to an existing lock is a widening. A pack entry in a lock written before permissions were recorded has none; it counts as the baseline only while the pack's files still hash as that lock says, and never for MCP servers and their hosts, since mcp/servers.toml isn't among the hashed files. install --frozen installs only what the lock records, so it never asks and takes no --yes: a widening fails it, and apply is where to review and accept it.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
The plan lives in GitHub epics: each one groups sub-issues in build order and says how to run them with Gatework's spec-agent (/brainrc-work --campaign gh:<epic>). This page lists every open epic under the release gate it belongs to, matching the GitHub milestones, in the order to start them. Within a gate, the epic's own "Start after" note wins over this order. An epic whose children span two gates sits under the gate where most of its open work is, and its line names the child that sits elsewhere.

A sub-issue's Roadmap ID says where it belongs: GA-, GB- or GC- for Gate A, B or C, and P0- to P4- for the earlier waves 0 to 4, which the gates replaced.

Shipped work is in the CHANGELOG. A closed epic drops off the lists; each gate's first line names the epics it has shipped.

docs.title: Gate A: public launch
docs.text: Shipped in this gate: E4, E5, E6, E27 (lockfile), E28 (trust baseline) and E29 (pack naming). Gate A's standalone issues, with no epic, are in its milestone. - D1 Owner decisions and accounts: the name, the namespace, PyPI and release accounts. A person does these, not an agent.

docs.title: Gate B: v1.0
docs.text:

  • E7 Pack scaffolding: new pack, a pack template repo, and pack author docs.
  • E8 Item scaffolders: new skill, new agent, new rule and new command.
  • E12 Importers: Windsurf rules and Claude plugins as packs, after the Gate A importers for CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Cursor and Copilot.
  • E10 Pack extension points: a [scope] predicate, declarative guard rules, pack-owned settings keys and reviewers, mode overrides, and unavailable gates.
  • E11 Guard parity across harnesses: the declarative guard rules evaluated in every tool, compiled to OS sandbox settings, and a security-baseline pack.
  • E31 Adapter SDK and more tools: an adapter plugin interface, then Copilot, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Kiro, Amp and Junie.
  • E20 Stack packs: official packs (starter, review, Go, Terraform, Kubernetes, Python, Node/TypeScript, Rust), and domain skills moved out of core.
  • E16 Native Windows: copy mode instead of symlinks, native hook commands, and a Windows CI cell.
  • E15 Split and 1.0: freeze the pack API, move specs/ out of the way, and tag v1.0. Its README and concepts child (#296) is Gate A.
  • E21 Pack index and pack evals: evals for packs, a searchable index, signing tiers, a publish scanner and badges. Its verified vendor packs child (#333) is Gate C.
  • E14 pack-builder skill: an interview that plans and generates your own pack, with an eval case.

docs.title: Gate C: team adoption
docs.text:
• E32 Teams and org policy: an org manifest, a brainrc check GitHub Action, and an agent bill of materials.
  • E33 Cloud and parallel agents: cloud agents and devcontainers set up from the lockfile, and loaded config verified by hash.
  • E13 Facts and freshness: a built-in facts pattern with verified dates, and an audit for stale ones.
  • E19 Plugin export and graduation: export a pack as a plugin, plugin dependencies, and a guide for graduating a pack.
  • E23 Unattended runs: run budgets, stacked PRs whose run records reach main, and concurrent runs.
  • E24 Repo context and the quality loop: a codemap, lint hooks after edits, retro lessons promoted to rules, and a second-opinion reviewer. Its core-evals-in-CI child (#249) is Gate B.

  • E17 Live checks for the native harness packages: run each harness package in a real, logged-in session.
